idiom_name: hand-written wrapper struct (named target field, one gated method per interface member) + sync/atomic.Bool
implementation_notes: Go has no dynamic proxies, so the forwarder is a struct with a named field holding the target plus one method per interface member, each loading an atomic flag (or taking a mutex) and forwarding or returning an error. Do not embed the interface to save those methods: embedding promotes the target's methods directly into the wrapper's method set, and those promoted calls never consult the flag. Publication is part of the design - the memory model only guarantees visibility through synchronization such as the atomics in sync/atomic or a mutex - so a plain bool flipped by the revoker goroutine is a data race, and drain semantics are a sync.RWMutex with the revoker taking the write lock.
pitfalls: Embedding the interface in the wrapper promotes every method straight to the target, so calls bypass the flag entirely (promoted methods are part of the wrapper's method set); a named field forces the gated methods to be written.

A non-atomic flag is a data race: the Go memory model guarantees visibility only through synchronization (atomics, mutexes, channels), so the revoker's write may never be observed by the forwarding goroutine.
Returning the wrapper by value copies the flag, so revocation performed on the grantor's copy leaves the collaborator's copy live; always hand out a pointer to the one shared wrapper.
